unit-bio-u1b.title: Biology 8 · Unit 1 Part 2: Data Analysis and Graphing
unit-bio-u1b.srcName: Experimental Design & Data Analysis unit slides and the graphing practice sheet (Drive)
unit-bio-u1b.source: Biology 8, Unit 1 — 'G8 Experimental Design 2026-27' slides and '03 graphing practice with grid' (Drive)

summary.text: The second half of the Unit 1 slides, picking up where the variables section ends. How many levels an independent variable has, and why controlled variables are not the same thing as a control group. Accuracy against reliability — a measurement can be one without the other. Then the statistics: mean, median and mode, what an outlier does to each, why an outlier is never simply deleted, and what a standard deviation is telling you. Finally the graphing rules — independent variable on the x-axis, line graphs for continuous data and bar graphs for discrete, sensible scaling, honest titles, and how to read a value or calculate a rate off a finished graph.

why.text: Designing the experiment is half the job; the other half is not fooling yourself with the results. One freak reading can drag a mean somewhere untrue, and the wrong graph can hide the pattern you collected the data to find. These are the moves that decide whether your conclusion is worth anything.

objectives.text: Count the levels of an independent variable, and tell controlled variables from the control group.
Distinguish accuracy from reliability and say which a given result demonstrates.
Calculate mean, median and mode, and say which best represents a data set.
Identify an outlier, explain its effect on the mean, and say why it stays in the data.
Choose the right graph type, set the axes correctly, and read a value or a rate off a graph.

parentNote.text: This is Part 2 rather than an edit to the existing Unit 1 unit. The two files added to the Biology Unit 1 folder today are a much fuller slide deck than the one the first unit was built from, and roughly half of it is new ground — levels of a variable, accuracy versus reliability, mean/median/mode, outliers, standard deviation, and the graphing rules in detail. Folding it in would have pushed that unit past thirty cards and re-drafted a unit already approved; a companion unit adds the material without disturbing it, and nothing here contradicts what is already there. The graphs are drawn from the slides' own data sets — the bird-count week, the electric bills, and the CO₂ growth experiment from the graphing practice sheet — so the numbers are the teacher's, though the questions asked about them are fresh. I checked the deck's own statistics: mean 113.6, median 114.5 and the bimodal 101/116 for the electric bills are all correct, as are mean 24, median 15 and mode 9 for the bird week. The thing most likely to trip her up is that a controlled variable and a control group are different things with confusingly similar names — the slides flag it explicitly, and so does a card here.

nextUp.text: Run the cards, then the quiz. The outlier questions are the ones worth slowing down on — they are where a wrong answer is still a plausible number.

cards.def:
**How many different values of the independent variable you test.**
• Testing ages 5, 10 and 15 is one variable with three levels.
• Testing 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15 is still one variable — now with six levels.
• More levels means a finer picture of the pattern.
cards.hint: One variable, many levels. Changing the number of levels is not the same as adding a second variable.

cards.term: Controlled variables are not the control group
cards.def:
**Controlled variables are the things kept the same; the control group is the group that gets no treatment.**
• Controlled variables: same quiz, same room, same time of day.
• Control group: the class that had no music playing at all.
• The names are almost identical and the meanings are not. The slides flag this on purpose.
cards.hint: Controlled variables are conditions. A control group is a group of subjects.

cards.term: The control group is a level too
cards.def:
**The untreated group counts as one level of the independent variable.**
• Walking, running, weights, yoga and no exercise is five levels, not four.
• It is the level that shows you what normal looks like.
cards.hint: Doing nothing is a treatment condition. Count it.

cards.def:
**How close a result is to the known, accepted value.**
• The scale reads 3.5 kg and the object really is 3.5 kg — that is accurate.
• Accuracy needs a true value to compare against.
cards.hint: Accurate = correct. It is about hitting the target.

cards.def:
**How consistent a result is when the measurement is repeated.**
• Weigh the object five times on five scales and get 3.5 kg every time — that is reliable.
• Reliability needs repetition, not a true value.
cards.hint: Reliable = repeatable. It is about grouping tightly, wherever you hit.

cards.def:
**A measurement can be one without the other.**
• Five scales all reading 4.0 kg for a 3.5 kg object: reliable, but not accurate.
• Readings scattered around 3.5 kg that average out right: accurate on average, but not reliable.
• A good experiment wants both.
cards.hint: Consistently wrong is still consistent. That is why reliability alone proves nothing.

cards.def:
**The average — add every value, then divide by how many there are.**
• The most commonly used summary of a data set.
• It uses every value, which is its strength and also its weakness.
cards.hint: Every number pulls on the mean, including the strange ones.

cards.def:
**The middle value once the numbers are put in order.**
• Odd count: the middle number. Even count: the average of the middle two.
• You must sort the list first — this is the step people skip.
cards.hint: Median = middle. Sort before you look.

cards.def:
**The value that appears most often.**
• A data set can have no mode at all, or more than one.
• The electric-bill set has two: $101 and $116 both appear twice.
cards.hint: Mode = most. It is the only one of the three that must be a value actually in the list.

cards.def:
**A data point that sits far away from all the others.**
• 87 birds on Thursday when every other day is between 9 and 18.
• It is a signal to investigate, not a mistake to assume.
cards.hint: An outlier is a question, not an error.

cards.term: What an outlier does to each statistic
cards.def:
**It drags the mean and leaves the median almost untouched.**
• Bird week: mean 24, median 15 — the mean is higher than six of the seven days.
• The median only cares about position in the order, so one extreme value barely moves it.
cards.hint: When mean and median disagree sharply, suspect an outlier.

cards.def:
**An outlier may carry the most important information in the data set.**
• The 87-bird Thursday is probably the migration arriving — the very thing being studied.
• Removing it because it is inconvenient would delete the discovery.
cards.hint: Investigate it, explain it, keep it. Deleting data to tidy a graph is not science.

cards.def:
**A number for how spread out the data is around the mean.**
• Low standard deviation: values cluster tightly. High: they are scattered.
• Two data sets can share a mean of 80 and have standard deviations of 3.4 and 17.2 — very different stories.
cards.hint: The mean says where the middle is; the standard deviation says how much to trust it.

cards.def:
**Independent variable on the left, dependent variable in the columns beside it.**
• Units go in the column headings, not repeated in every cell.
• Be consistent — pick one place for the units and stay there.
cards.hint: The table should read left to right in the same order as the experiment: what you changed, then what happened.

cards.term: Which variable goes on which axis
cards.def:
**Independent variable on the x-axis, dependent variable on the y-axis.**
• The thing you chose goes along the bottom; the thing you measured goes up the side.
• Getting this backwards makes an otherwise perfect graph unreadable.
cards.hint: x is what you did, y is what happened.

cards.def:
**Line for continuous data, bar for discrete categories.**
• The test: could there be a real value BETWEEN two of your x-values?
• Speed each minute of one drive — yes, 3.5 minutes exists, so line graph.
• Average speed of five separate drives — no, there is no drive 3.5, so bar graph.
cards.hint: Ask whether the space between two points means anything. If it does, join them.

cards.def:
**Every gridline must step up by the same amount.**
• 0, 20, 40, 60 is a scale. 0, 20, 50, 60 is not.
• Uneven spacing distorts the shape of the data, which is the one thing a graph exists to show honestly.
cards.hint: A constant step per line, chosen so the data fills most of the space.

cards.def:
**Descriptive enough for someone who was not there to understand it.**
• 'Time versus speed' is not enough.
• 'Time in seconds required to complete a 100-piece puzzle, by grade' is.
• Check above AND below the graph — titles are placed in both.
cards.hint: If the title could sit on twenty different graphs, it is too vague.

cards.term: Reading a graph in the right order
cards.def:
**Title first, then the axes and their units, then the data.**
• Almost everyone looks at the line first, and that is how units get missed.
• Use a straight edge when estimating a value between gridlines.
cards.hint: Three steps before you read a single data point.

cards.term: Getting a rate off a graph
cards.def:
**Change in the y-value divided by the change in the x-value.**
• Heart rate goes from 98 to 121 bpm between minutes 2 and 4: a change of 23 bpm.
• Over 2 minutes that is 11.5 bpm per minute.
• The word 'per' is the instruction to divide.
cards.hint: Overall change and change per unit are two different questions. Read which one is being asked.

cards.def:
**A trend line should not be forced through your first and last data points.**
• It represents the whole set, not the two points that happen to sit at the ends.
• On graph paper: ruler, pencil, no markers.
cards.hint: If your line hits the first and last points exactly, you drew a connector, not a fit.

questions.q: What is the median of this data set: 9, 9, 14, 15, 16, 18, 87?
questions.hint: Seven values, already in order. Which position is the middle?
steps: The list is already sorted from smallest to largest.
There are seven values, so the middle one is the fourth.
Counting in: 9, 9, 14, then 15 is the fourth value.
So the median is 15. The 24 is this set's mean and the 9 is its mode.

ex.main: **15.** With an odd count the median is simply the middle value once sorted. Here the mean is 24 and the mode is 9 — three different answers from the same seven numbers.
ex.tip: Sort first, every time. An unsorted list makes the median look like whatever sits in the middle of the page.

questions.q: A set of values has no number appearing more than once. What is its mode?
opts: Zero
The mean instead
There is no mode
The smallest value
questions.hint: Mode means most frequent. What if nothing repeats?
steps: The mode is the value that occurs most often.
If every value appears exactly once, none occurs more often than another.
So the set simply has no mode — that is a valid outcome.
A mode of zero would mean the number 0 appeared most, which is a different claim.

ex.main: **There is no mode.** Not every data set has one, and some have several — the electric-bill set is bimodal at $101 and $116.
ex.tip: No mode is an answer. Do not force one by rounding values until something repeats.

questions.q: Which variable belongs on the x-axis of a graph?
opts: The independent variable
The dependent variable
Whichever has larger numbers
The controlled variable
questions.hint: Along the bottom goes the thing you chose to change.
steps: The x-axis is the horizontal one, along the bottom.
By convention it carries the variable the experimenter set deliberately.
That is the independent variable.
The dependent variable — the thing measured — goes up the y-axis.

ex.main: **The independent variable.** x is what you did, y is what happened. Controlled variables do not go on either axis; they are held constant.
ex.tip: If a graph looks strange, check the axes before you doubt the data.

questions.q: A scale reads 3.5 kg five separate times for an object known to weigh 3.5 kg. This demonstrates:
opts: Reliability only — the readings simply agree
Accuracy only — it matches the known value
Both accuracy and reliability at once
Neither, since one scale was used repeatedly
questions.hint: Two different claims are being made here — check for each one separately.
steps: Reliability is consistency across repeats: five identical readings, so yes.
Accuracy is closeness to the accepted value: 3.5 kg matches the known 3.5 kg, so yes.
Both conditions are satisfied at once.
Had it read 4.0 kg five times, it would be reliable but not accurate.

ex.main: **Both.** The readings agree with each other (reliable) and with the true value (accurate). Testing each separately is the habit worth building.
ex.tip: Consistently wrong is still consistent — which is why reliability alone never proves a result.

questions.q: An experiment tests plant growth under white, red, yellow, green, blue and purple light. How many levels does the independent variable have?
opts: One
Two
Six
Thirty
questions.hint: One variable is being changed. Count how many versions of it were tested.
steps: The independent variable is the colour of the light — one variable.
Count the different values tested: white, red, yellow, green, blue, purple.
That is six different settings, so six levels.
It is still one variable, no matter how many levels it has.

ex.main: **Six.** One variable, six levels. Adding levels sharpens the picture; adding a second variable would ruin the experiment.
ex.tip: Levels answer 'how many versions', not 'how many variables'.

questions.q: What does a standard deviation tell you about a data set?
opts: Which value occurs most often
How spread out the values are
The middle value in the set
How many values were collected
questions.hint: It is a companion to the mean, not a replacement.
steps: Standard deviation measures how far values sit from the mean on average.
A small one means the data clusters tightly around the mean.
A large one means the values are widely scattered.
The most common value is the mode and the middle one is the median — different questions.

ex.main: **How spread out the values are.** Two classes can both average 80 with deviations of 3.4 and 17.2 — same mean, completely different stories.
ex.tip: Always read a mean alongside its spread. A mean on its own hides how typical it really is.

questions.q: A student measures average speed for five separate car journeys. Which graph should she use?
opts: A line graph
A bar graph
A pie chart
A scatterplot with a best-fit line
questions.hint: Is there such a thing as journey number 3.5?
steps: Ask whether values exist between the x-values.
The journeys are separate events — there is no drive between the third and the fourth.
That makes the data discrete, so the categories should not be joined by a line.
Discrete categories are drawn as a bar graph.

ex.main: **A bar graph.** The journeys are separate categories, so the space between them means nothing. Speed measured each minute WITHIN one drive would be continuous, and that would be a line graph.
ex.tip: The in-between test decides it every time: does a value between these two x-values exist?

questions.q: A week of bird counts is shown in the graph. The mean is 24 and the median is 15. Why are they so far apart?
opts: The mean was calculated incorrectly here
There are too few days to take a mean from
Thursday's 87 is an outlier lifting the mean
The median only works on even-sized sets
questions.hint: Which of the two statistics uses every value?
steps: Six of the seven days sit between 9 and 18; Thursday is 87.
The mean adds every value, so one huge number lifts the whole total.
The median depends only on position in the sorted order, so an extreme value barely shifts it.
The result is a mean of 24 that is higher than six of the seven actual days.

ex.main: **Thursday's 87 is an outlier, and only the mean feels it.** When mean and median disagree sharply, an outlier is the first thing to look for.
ex.tip: A mean higher than most of the individual values is a red flag worth chasing.

questions.q: A week of bird counts runs 15, 16, 9, 87, 18, 14 and 9, giving a mean of 24, a median of 15 and a mode of 9. Which statistic best represents a typical day, and why?
opts: The mean, because it uses every value
The mode, because it is a real count
The median, because the outlier barely moves it
The standard deviation, because it is precise
questions.hint: Which one lands closest to what most of the days actually looked like?
steps: Look at what a typical day was: six of the seven days fall between 9 and 18 birds.
The mean of 24 sits above six of those seven days, so it is not typical of any of them.
The median of 15 lands right among them.
The mode of 9 is the joint-lowest count, so it under-represents the week.

ex.main: **The median.** It resists the outlier and lands where most days actually were. The mean is not wrong — it is just answering a different question.
ex.tip: 'Best represents' means closest to typical, not most precise.

questions.q: Groups of students take a quiz with classical, jazz, country, rock, or no music. Which is a controlled variable rather than the control group?
opts: The group with no music playing
The type of music each group heard
Every group taking the same quiz
The average score each group achieved
questions.hint: Controlled variables are conditions held steady, not a group of people.
steps: The independent variable is the type of music, and the dependent variable is the score.
The control group is the one receiving no treatment — the silent group.
A controlled variable is a condition kept identical for everyone, such as using the same quiz.
So the same quiz is a controlled variable; the silent group is the control group.

ex.main: **Every group taking the same quiz.** Controlled variables are conditions; a control group is a set of subjects. The slides flag this pair because the names are so easy to swap.
ex.tip: Ask 'is this a condition or a group of subjects?' — that settles it instantly.

questions.q: Five scales each read 4.0 kg for an object known to weigh 3.5 kg. What does this show?
opts: Reliable but not accurate
Accurate but not reliable
Both accurate and reliable
Neither, since the readings agree
questions.hint: Test the two properties one at a time.
steps: Check reliability: all five readings agree with each other, so it is reliable.
Check accuracy: 4.0 kg does not match the accepted 3.5 kg, so it is not accurate.
The result is consistent and consistently wrong.
This usually points to a systematic problem, such as scales that all need recalibrating.

ex.main: **Reliable but not accurate.** Agreement between repeats says nothing about whether the value is right — which is exactly why both properties get separate names.
ex.tip: Repeating a measurement improves reliability. Only checking against a known value improves accuracy.

questions.q: In the graph shown, at roughly what CO₂ concentration do animal and plant cells grow at the same rate?
questions.hint: Find where the two curves cross.
steps: Two series are plotted: one falls as CO₂ rises, the other climbs.
Equal growth means the point where the two lines meet.
They cross at 0.04%, where both sit at 100%/day.
That value is the concentration of CO₂ in ordinary atmosphere — which is why both are normalised to 100 there.

ex.main: **0.04%, where both reach 100%/day.** That is atmospheric CO₂, the baseline both cell types are measured against — so the crossing point is built into the experiment's design.
ex.tip: On a two-series graph, the crossing point is almost always the question worth asking.

questions.q: In the graph shown, what happens to the two cell types as CO₂ rises above the atmospheric level of 0.04%?
opts: Both grow faster
Both slow down
Animal cells slow down while plant cells speed up
Animal cells speed up while plant cells slow down
questions.hint: Follow each line to the right and note which way it goes.
steps: Take the line that starts high on the left: it falls steadily, ending near 9%/day.
Take the line that starts at zero: it climbs steadily, ending above 200%/day.
Plants use CO₂ for photosynthesis, so the rising line is the plant cells.
So above 0.04%, animal growth falls and plant growth rises.

ex.main: **Animal cells slow, plant cells speed up.** Plants consume CO₂ and animals are poisoned by an excess of it, so the same change moves the two in opposite directions.
ex.tip: When two series cross, do not describe them as one trend. State what each does separately.

questions.q: A student measures the mass of mitochondria, nucleus and Golgi in three different cell types. Which graph suits this data?
opts: A line graph, since the cells can be ordered
A bar graph, since the cell types are separate categories
A scatterplot with a line of best fit
A single line per organelle, joined across cell types
questions.hint: Is there a cell type between a myocyte and an endocrine cell?
steps: Apply the in-between test to the x-axis categories.
Myocyte, endocrine and epithelial are distinct cell types, not points on a scale.
There is no cell halfway between two of them, so the data is discrete.
Discrete categories are drawn as bars, grouped by organelle.

ex.main: **A bar graph.** The cell types are categories, so joining them with a line would imply a progression that does not exist. The CO₂ data is different — concentration is continuous, so that one gets a fitted line.
ex.tip: One sheet can need both graph types. Test each data set separately rather than picking one style for the page.

questions.q: A family's twelve electric bills have mean $113.60 and median $114.50. If August's bill had been $351 instead of $145, what happens to those two statistics?
opts: Both statistics rise by roughly seventeen dollars
Mean rises to about $130.80; median unchanged
The median rises while the mean stays put
Neither moves, since only one value changed
questions.hint: One statistic uses every value; the other only uses position.
steps: The mean uses the total, so adding $206 to one bill adds $206 to the total.
$206 spread over twelve months raises the mean by about $17, to roughly $130.80.
The median depends only on the middle two values in the sorted list.
August was already the highest bill and stays the highest, so the middle of the order does not move and the median remains $114.50.

ex.main: **Mean up to about $130.80, median unchanged at $114.50.** One extreme value moves the mean and leaves the median where it was — the clearest demonstration of why both get reported.
ex.tip: Before calculating, ask whether the changed value crossed the middle of the order. If it did not, the median cannot move.

questions.q: A researcher finds one wildly high value in a week of data. What should be done with it?
opts: Delete it, since it distorts the mean
Keep it and investigate what caused it
Replace it with the median of the other values
Repeat only that day until a normal value appears
questions.hint: What might a strange reading actually be telling you?
steps: An outlier can come from a measurement error or from something genuinely happening.
You cannot tell which without investigating the cause.
In the bird data, the spike is most likely the migration arriving — the very thing being studied.
Deleting or replacing it would erase the finding, so it stays in the data and gets explained.

ex.main: **Keep it and find out why.** Removing data because it is inconvenient is how a real discovery gets thrown away. Report it, explain it, and note its effect on the mean.
ex.tip: Repeating only the measurement you dislike, until it agrees with you, is the same error wearing a lab coat.

questions.q: The graph shows a student's heart rate each minute while exercising. Approximately how much did it change per minute between minutes 2 and 4?
opts: 23 bpm per minute
11.5 bpm per minute
121 bpm per minute
2 bpm per minute
questions.hint: The word 'per' is an instruction to divide.
steps: Read the two values: about 98 bpm at minute 2 and about 121 bpm at minute 4.
The overall change is 121 − 98 = 23 bpm.
That change happened over 4 − 2 = 2 minutes.
Per minute, that is 23 ÷ 2 = 11.5 bpm per minute. The 23 on its own answers a different question.

ex.main: **11.5 bpm per minute.** The total change is 23 bpm; dividing by the two minutes turns it into a rate. Both numbers are correct answers to different questions, so read which one was asked.
ex.tip: 'Overall change' and 'change per minute' differ by one division. The wrong one is always on offer.

questions.q: Two classes both average 80% on a quiz. Class A's standard deviation is 3.4 and Class B's is 17.2. What does that tell you?
opts: Class A scored higher overall than Class B did
Class B simply has more students than Class A
Class A clusters near 80; Class B is spread wide
Class B's mean must have been miscalculated
questions.hint: The means are identical, so the difference is not about the middle.
steps: Both classes share a mean of 80, so neither scored higher on average.
Standard deviation describes spread around that mean, not its position.
A deviation of 3.4 means most scores sit within a few points of 80.
A deviation of 17.2 means scores range widely — some far above 80 and some far below.

ex.main: **Same average, very different classes.** In A almost everyone is near 80; in B the 80 is an average of high and low scores, and may describe nobody at all.
ex.tip: A mean without a spread can hide two opposite situations. Ask for both.

questions.q: A graph's y-axis runs 0, 20, 50, 60, 100. What is wrong with it, and why does it matter?
opts: Uneven steps distort the shape of the data
It should start at zero, and it already does
There are too few gridlines to read values from
The axis needs category labels instead of numbers
questions.hint: Measure the gap between each pair of labels.
steps: Check the gaps: 20, then 30, then 10, then 40 — all different.
A graph's vertical distances are supposed to be proportional to the values.
With uneven steps, equal distances on the page represent unequal changes in the data.
So the line's shape misleads, which defeats the point of drawing it.

ex.main: **Uneven steps distort the shape.** A graph's job is to make the pattern visible honestly; inconsistent spacing makes rises look like plateaus and vice versa. This axis does start at zero — that part is fine.
ex.tip: Check the gaps between gridline labels before reading any graph, including ones in the news.

questions.q: An investigation compares walking, running, weights, yoga and no exercise. How many levels does the independent variable have, and which is the control?
opts: Four levels; no-exercise is separate from the levels
Five levels; no-exercise is the control group
Five levels; there is no control group here
Four levels; running is the control group
questions.hint: Does the untreated group count as a level?
steps: The independent variable is the type of exercise.
List the conditions tested: walking, running, weights, yoga, and none — five in total.
The untreated condition counts as a level, so there are five.
That untreated group is the control, showing how heart rate varies without any exercise at all.

ex.main: **Five levels, with no-exercise as the control.** Doing nothing is a real condition being compared against, so it counts. Without it you would have nothing to measure the other four against.
ex.tip: Count the control group when counting levels. It is the level that defines normal.

questions.q: Why should a line of best fit not be drawn through the first and last data points exactly?
opts: Those two points are usually measured wrongly
A best-fit line must pass through the origin
Two points would then decide the entire line
A best-fit line should touch no data points
questions.hint: What would the middle points contribute if the ends fixed the line?
steps: A best-fit line is meant to represent every point in the data set.
Forcing it through the first and last points fixes the line using only those two.
Every measurement in between would then have no influence at all.
That is connecting endpoints rather than fitting, and it hands all the weight to two readings that carry the same random error as the rest.

ex.main: **Those two points would decide everything.** A fit is supposed to average out the scatter across all the data. It may happen to pass through some points — it just must not be forced to.
ex.tip: A trend line represents the set. If any single point can move it much, it is not a fit.
